I posit that the likelihood that the likelihood of a published paper discusses racial inequality is driven by two mechanisms: the volume of submissions journals receives on the topic and the probability that such submissions are accepted.

I suggest that three variables influence both mechanisms. First, social science journals is a particularly receptive venue for inequality scholarship. These outlets not only attract more submissions on such topics but also show greater editorial openness to publishing this work. Second, paper_inequality_mentions_3_years captures the salience of the inequality topic. When a topic gets more attention, journals are more likely to receive related submissions and more inclined to publish them. Third, news_inequality_mentions_3_years reflects public attention to inequality. Media coverage may stimulate scholarly interest in the topic, thereby increasing submission rates, while simultaneously signaling to editors the broader relevance of such work, potentially enhancing acceptance likelihood. I assume that journal focus has a stronger direct influence than broad scholarly attention, which in turn has a stronger influence than public attention.

I also include two additional variables to capture individual-level interest in racial inequality. First, I consider country_race_diversity_score, as individuals in more racially diverse environments are likely to be more exposed to discussions of racial inequality. Second, I focus on Black, which I perceive as one of the most prominently discussed forms of racial inequality globally. I prioritized country_race_diversity_score over Black because not all Black individuals reside in racially heterogeneous settings while racial diversity captures a broader contextual dimension.

I posit that the likelihood that a published paper addresses racial inequality is driven by the supply of and demand for scholarship on this topic. On the demand side, journal receptivity is central. Social science journals, in particular, are particularly receptive venues for inequality research: they both attract a higher volume of submissions on racial inequality and exhibit a greater propensity to publish such work. On the supply side, individual scholarly interest shapes the supply of gender inequality works. Interest in gender inequality stems from both general and specific sources. General interest arises among scholars attentive to inequality broadly, including those focused on racial inequality, suggesting a spillover effect across inequality domains. Specific interest emerges among scholars directly engaged with gender inequality discourse, reflecting targeted attention to this particular form of stratification.

Second-order interactions reflect a core emphasis on disciplinary amplification. Similarly, the positive social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years interaction reflects the idea that social sciences are particularly responsive to societal and media attention, so external inequality salience amplifies their tendency to produce gender-focused work. Thus, the theory emphasizes disciplinary context as the primary amplifier of inequality salience, while recognizing that the influence of female authorship is context-dependent and relatively stronger in fields where gender inequality is not already normative.

My theory is that first and foremost, articles on inequality are published in social science journals. That's just a base rate -- the topic of social science journals are social topics, and diversity / racial inequality is more a a social topic than anything else. The mechanism here isn't anything psychological but statistical so I am not including a mediator.

Second, inequality being part of the "zeitgeist" (via news articles) will increase its salience and permissibility/popularity (i.e., it is "OK" to write about) in the minds of all researchers -- much like "AI" is all over the news these days. Trends in publications follow trends in what is important in society (e.g., intros and discussion sections usually refer to these, researchers get ideas from everyday life, etc.).

Third, I believe that one's own racial identity may motivate one to research in equality, partly due to a salience argument (as above - if you experience it in your everyday life, you will have more inspiration to research it and tackle it) and partly due to motivation (you likely want to help reduce it for future generations, your kids, your family, your friends, etc.). I have a lay intuition that personal motivation may appear higher for people who identify as Black and Asian, because a larger percentage of published research comes from the US, UK, and China. Since I could only list five factors though, I chose to focus on Black as it seems that is a more dominant racial identity studied in the literature (at least based on my narrow reading/memory of it). I also didn't include Hispanic/Other merely from a statistical prevalence and time standpoint. While that ethnicity surely has faced terrible discrimination recently under the Trump administration with deportations, any motivational or salience mechanism won't appear in the published literature until maybe late 2026 or 2027, which is later than this survey. Further, that population is smaller so it may not have enough power to get picked up on in models.

Fourth, I included Female partly due to my own "sampling". I have no idea if this is true in the population, but it seems that people studying diversity of any kind in my network tend to be female. Sometimes they study gender diversity but often they also study racial diversity. I think the mechanism is actually quite similar to race though: Women may feel more discriminated against (Salience) and want to change that (Motivation) including for social categories not their own (Prosocial).

Finally, I ranked publication prevalence lower than news prevalence because my hunch is the former lags behind the latter -- i.e., researchers' interests are inspired by the news more than the news is inspired by researchers' interests. That said, once a theme becomes popular in publications, it does tend to create a trend (e.g., how we talk about in every job market cycle there are "hot" topics - diversity was "hot" a few years ago, AI is hot now). So it does have influence - just lagged and less so than the news, I think. Here I think the mediator is salience, permissibility / popularity, and motivation (ie if past articles were published on this future articles like mine will be too).

In terms of interaction effects, I believe that news and publication trends will heighten the mechanisms with one's own race (or gender). I.e., in a causal diagram, and arrow would flow from each (news, publication) to the arrow between race (black) or gender (female) to the Y variable.

For starters, I assumed that if an author is a woman or Black, that probably increases the chances their work engages with racial inequality. Not because of any hard rule, but just because people's backgrounds and experiences tend to shape what they find interesting or important. If you've lived some of those realities yourself, or you're just more tuned in to questions of justice and fairness, it makes sense you might gravitate toward those topics. That's not just an academic guess, it's pretty intuitive.

I also thought that researchers working in more racially diverse countries would be more likely to write about racial inequality. The logic there is pretty straightforward: if you're surrounded by those conversations in everyday life, they're more likely to show up in your work.

On the flip side, I gave negative signs to how much inequality shows up in the news or in other academic papers from the previous few years. Why? Because a lot of that talk tends to be about inequality more broadly, income, gender, region, not race specifically. So if there's a lot of generic "inequality" chatter floating around, it might actually dilute the focus on racial inequality rather than boost it. A paper might mention inequality in passing without ever zooming in on race.

So in the end, the ranking basically reflects this idea: the strongest drivers are probably the researchers themselves, who they are and what they bring to the table. The broader context matters too, but it's more of a background factor, and sometimes the signal gets muddied.

Asian authors may also be positive predictors because Asian scholars may be engaging with racial dynamics in their own contexts, whether that is anti-Asian discrimination, colonialism, or immigration. Identity is more complicated than a simple US Black-white frame. Who you are shapes what you study, but where you are, the field you work in, and how the model sees you matter just as much.

The positive sign for female_score underscores the importance of author demographics in shaping research agendas, as scholars' identities and lived experiences influence the questions they ask and the issues they prioritize. Asian authors are also significant contributors to research on gender inequality, whether due to their experiences with gender disparities in academic or professional settings, their engagement with gender issues in Asian societies, or their involvement in global or comparative gender studies. This highlights the global and intersectional nature of gender inequality research, where scholars from diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds bring unique perspectives and priorities to the study of gender dynamics. It also suggests that gender inequality is not solely a "Western" concern but a topic of broad, cross-cultural relevance, with contributions from scholars embedded in a variety of socio-political contexts. Natural science disciplines, which prioritize empirical, technical, or biological questions, are less likely to engage with gender inequality unless it directly intersects with their core research, such as studies of gender disparities in STEM participation. This negative effect underscores the idea that disciplinary culture acts as a filter, shaping which topics are deemed relevant or legitimate within a given field. While natural scientists may study gender disparities in specific contexts, such as workforce representation or educational outcomes, these discussions are less central to the disciplines' overall research agendas compared to social science fields. Paper_inequality_mentions_3_years highlights the self-reinforcing nature of academic discourse. When gender inequality is a prominent topic in the scholarly literature, it signals to researchers that the issue is timely, relevant, and worthy of attention. This creates a cumulative advantage, where initial interest in a topic begets further research, amplifying its visibility and importance within the academic community. Scholars may be more responsive to internal academic trends than to external public discourse, at least in the context of gender inequality research. This may reflect the insularity of academic research agendas or the fact that scholars are more attuned to the priorities of their peers, funding agencies, and disciplinary traditions than to broader societal conversations. In summary, the factors driving academic engagement with gender inequality emphasize the interplay of disciplinary norms, author demographics, and academic discourse, while also highlighting the global and intersectional dimensions of gender inequality research. The role of Asian authors expands the theoretical framework to recognize the diverse and cross-cultural contributions to this area of study, while the negative effect of natural_science reinforces the importance of disciplinary context in shaping research priorities. Together, these factors provide a more comprehensive and inclusive account of how and why scholars engage with gender inequality in their work.

The selection and ranking of second-order interactions for predicting mentions of gender inequality in academic papers are grounded in theories of disciplinary norms, social identity, and the dynamic relationship between public discourse and scholarly research. The social_science × female interaction is considered the most important because it combines two of the strongest individual drivers of research focus: the disciplinary emphasis on gender and inequality, and the lived experiences or academic priorities of female authors. Social science fields, such as sociology, psychology, and gender studies, are explicitly designed to interrogate power structures, identity, and societal inequities, making them natural hubs for research on gender inequality. When female authors—who may have personal or professional stakes in gender issues—are part of these disciplines, the likelihood of addressing gender inequality is further amplified. This interaction reflects the idea that identity and disciplinary culture are not merely additive but multiplicative; the presence of female authors in social science contexts creates a synergistic effect, as their perspectives and priorities align with the field's focus on gender and inequality.

The social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years interaction is ranked second because it captures how social science disciplines, which are already attuned to societal issues, respond to broader public discourse. When gender inequality is prominently discussed in the news, it signals a heightened societal awareness and urgency, which can prompt scholars in these fields to engage with the topic in their research. Social science disciplines are particularly responsive to public conversations, as their methodologies and theoretical frameworks are often designed to address contemporary social issues. This interaction assumes that the alignment of disciplinary focus with public discourse creates a powerful impetus for scholarly engagement with gender inequality, reflecting the field's commitment to both academic rigor and societal relevance.

Finally, the female × authors_race_diversity_score interaction is ranked third, reflecting the intersectional dynamics that shape research agendas. Female authors, particularly those from diverse racial backgrounds, are more likely to bring intersectional perspectives to their work, recognizing how gender inequality intersects with other forms of marginalization. Diversity within author teams fosters a broader range of viewpoints and experiences, which can enrich the theoretical and empirical exploration of gender inequality. This interaction underscores the idea that diversity is not just a demographic feature but a catalyst for more nuanced and inclusive research. The positive sign for all these interactions assumes that the combination of female authorship, disciplinary focus, public discourse, and team diversity creates a fertile ground for addressing gender inequality in academic papers, highlighting the complex interplay of individual, disciplinary, and contextual factors in shaping research priorities.

Disciplinary norms, public discourse, academic discourse, and author demographics collectively shape the likelihood that an academic paper discusses gender inequality through second-order interactions. Social science disciplines act as powerful amplifiers for the effects of both academic and public discourse on gender inequality. The positive interactions between social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years suggest that social science fields are uniquely responsive to contemporary conversations about inequality. When gender inequality is prominently discussed in academic literature or public debates, social scientists are particularly likely to engage with the topic in their research. This aligns with theories of disciplinary norms and issue-attention cycles, where external stimuli, such as heightened academic or public focus, trigger increased scholarly engagement, especially in fields already oriented toward studying societal issues. Social science disciplines not only prioritize gender inequality as a research topic but also dynamically respond to shifts in broader conversations, whether within academia or in the public sphere. However, the negative interaction between female × social_science suggests that the marginal effect of female authorship on discussing gender inequality is smaller within social science fields, and conversely, the effect of being in a social science discipline is weaker when the share of female authors is higher. This counterintuitive relationship can be explained through several interconnected mechanisms. First, social science disciplines may already have a high baseline likelihood of discussing gender inequality, creating a "ceiling effect" that reduces the incremental impact of female authorship. Because gender inequality is already a central topic in these fields, the addition of female authors may not further amplify the likelihood of addressing it, as the discipline itself is already strongly oriented toward these issues. Second, female authors in social science fields may be more likely to specialize in specific subfields or topics that are adjacent to but distinct from the broad category of "gender inequality." For example, female scholars might focus on intersectional analyses, such as gender and race, class, or sexuality, feminist theory, or gender-related topics in specific domains, such as education, health, or labor markets. If whether a paper discusses gender inequality is defined narrowly, for example based on specific keywords, papers that take a more nuanced or intersectional approach may not be fully captured, leading to an apparent reduction in the effect of female authorship. Third, the negative interaction may reflect subfield dynamics within social science disciplines. Female authors might be overrepresented in subfields like gender studies, where the focus is on theoretical or qualitative analyses of gender, rather than empirical studies of gender inequality per se. Conversely, in subfields like economics or political science, where gender inequality is studied but not always central, female authors might prioritize other topics. This heterogeneity within social science disciplines could dilute the overall effect of female authorship on the likelihood of discussing gender inequality. Fourth, academic incentives and publication norms may shape how female scholars engage with gender inequality. Female authors in social science fields might face pressures to diversify their research portfolios or to focus on topics perceived as more "innovative" or "high-impact," which may not always align with studies of gender inequality. Alternatively, they may prioritize research that addresses gender inequality indirectly, for example through policy analyses, organizational studies, or cultural critiques, rather than explicitly, which could again lead to an underestimation of their engagement with the topic. Finally, female authors in social science disciplines may be more likely to study gender inequality in conjunction with other forms of inequality, such as racial or economic inequality, rather than in isolation. If discussions of gender inequality do not account for these intersectional analyses, female authors' contributions to broader or more complex discussions of inequality might not be fully captured. Overall, social science disciplines amplify the effects of academic and public discourse on gender inequality, while the role of female authorship within these disciplines is more complex than a simple positive additive relationship. Female scholars may engage with gender inequality in ways that are not fully captured by broad measures, whether through intersectional analyses, subfield specialization, or responses to academic incentives. This emphasizes the importance of considering not just whether gender inequality is discussed, but how and in what contexts, particularly when examining the role of author demographics and disciplinary norms.

My reasoning is anchored in a layered model of scholarly production, where a paper's topic is first and foremost shaped by the epistemological boundaries of its discipline, and then further modulated by the social positionality of its authors. At the foundational level, a discipline defines what constitutes a legitimate object of inquiry. Social science disciplines, such as sociology and political science, are built around the systematic study of social structures, power, and inequality; racial inequality is therefore not a peripheral concern but a central and theoretically prized subject. This makes social_science the most powerful positive predictor. The categorical opposite is equally informative: a paper in the natural_sciences is, by institutional and epistemological design, oriented toward biophysical processes rather than social ones, creating a powerful negative constraint on the likelihood of engaging with racial inequality discourse. This disciplinary context sets the broadest possible stage on which other factors operate. Operating within this stage, I draw on standpoint theory and the sociology of knowledge to argue that lived experience shapes scholarly attention. The share of black authors is my second-most important predictor because scholars from communities directly subordinated by racial hierarchy possess a distinctive "insider" perspective-a combination of personal motivation to understand and dismantle that hierarchy and privileged epistemic access to its nuances. This resounds as a strong positive signal, particularly given the anti-Black focus historically embedded in many racial inequality keywords. Extending this logic of positionality from the individual to the collaborative team, the authors_race_diversity_score captures a positive, dynamic effect. A racially heterogeneous team does not simply pool static identities; it creates a micro-social environment where contrasting perspectives must be negotiated, often sparking explicit inquiry into the very nature of racial difference and inequality that the team enacts. Finally, while the Black experience is a central axis of racial discourse, other marginalized groups also experience racialization; thus, a greater share of hispanic_and_other authors similarly predicts a higher likelihood of engaging the topic, though with a comparatively less consistent signal than the Black share given the keyword list's specific thematic gravity.

My theoretical framework retains the foundational logic that disciplinary context sets the stage for what can be studied, and author social position shapes the motivation and lens brought to inquiry, but it recognizes a broader, more globally distributed set of authorial positionalities and a cross-axis solidarity mechanism. At the broadest structural level, a paper's disciplinary home remains the most powerful determinant of whether it discusses racial inequality. Social science disciplines-sociology, political science, psychology, economics, history-are organized around the systematic study of social structures, power, and humanly constructed hierarchies. Racial inequality is thus not a peripheral topic but a central and theoretically prized object of inquiry, with dedicated journals, established theoretical frameworks, and professional incentives that actively reward such work. This disciplinary context provides the essential condition of possibility for racial inequality discourse in published academic work, and it operates prior to and more powerfully than any author-level characteristic. Author positionality matters not primarily through a single axis of identity but through a generalized inequality concern-a scholarly orientation toward social justice that can arise from multiple forms of marginalized experience. Women scholars, by virtue of their own encounters with gender-based subordination within academia and beyond, may develop a heightened sensitivity to hierarchy and exclusion in general. This is not simply empathy but a learned critical consciousness-an epistemic standpoint forged through navigating male-dominated institutional spaces-that makes the study of one form of inequality cognitively and affectively adjacent to the study of others. Moreover, the academic division of scholarly labor channels women disproportionately into inequality-focused subfields across multiple axes, a pattern sustained by both individual preference and structural sorting mechanisms such as mentoring networks and departmental expectations. This cross-axis mechanism means that female authorship is not merely a proxy for gender-focused research but a robust marker of broader engagement with social justice topics, including racial inequality. Racial inequality is also a genuinely global scholarly discourse, produced by researchers embedded in diverse national contexts where race and ethnicity are salient axes of social organization. Scholars from racially diverse countries-whether South Africa, Brazil, Malaysia, Singapore, or the United Kingdom-are socialized in environments where negotiating racial difference is a routine feature of public and institutional life. This socialization cultivates a scholarly attentiveness to race that travels with the researcher regardless of their specific national origin, and it provides a comparative lens that enriches and motivates engagement with the topic. Asian authorship can reflect multiple plausible pathways: Asian scholars in diaspora contexts studying racial dynamics in multiracial host societies; scholars in Asian societies with salient ethnic hierarchies (e.g., Malaysia, Singapore, India) applying frameworks of racial or ethnic inequality to their own contexts; and the growing internationalization of academic networks that brings scholars from Asia into collaborative projects on race. The geography of knowledge production shapes scholarly attention to race through a mechanism of contextual exposure-living and working in environments where race is visibly and discursively salient makes one more likely to see it as a legitimate and pressing object of study, irrespective of one's own racial category. Black author share remains important but sits within a broader constellation of positionalities rather than standing alone. The mechanism linking Black authorship to racial inequality discourse remains what standpoint theory would predict: direct, embodied experience of anti-Black racism provides both personal motivation and unique epistemic insight into the workings of racial hierarchy. Black scholars are a vital, concentrated source of this scholarship, but they operate within a global academic ecosystem where multiple identity pathways converge on the topic. The epistemological boundary between social and natural science is real, but the positive signal of social science is so powerful that the negative signal of natural science contributes relatively little additional predictive value. The compositional complexity of the team also matters less than the specific identity shares and the structural contexts from which authors are drawn. Collaborative diversity may be a consequence rather than a cause of engagement with racial inequality, or it may simply be too coarse a measure to capture the nuanced interpersonal dynamics hypothesized by team-level accounts.

My selection of these three interactions is governed by a hierarchical, structural-to-proximal logic, beginning with the foundational gatekeeping role of discipline and then moving to the more nuanced internal dynamics of author teams. The most important interaction, social_science × black, captures what I see as the essential synergy between motivational capacity and institutional opportunity. My core assumption is that a scholar's propensity to study racial inequality is not a simple function of identity or disciplinary context alone, but of their conjunction. A Black scholar carries, on average, a heightened personal stake in understanding racial subordination, but this motivation requires a disciplinary home that legitimizes such inquiry as rigorous scholarship to be fully realized in published output. Social science provides precisely this scaffolding-its journals, peer networks, and theoretical canons offer a receptive structure that amplifies the expression of standpoint-driven motivation. In a natural science or engineering field, an equally motivated Black scholar faces a disciplinary environment where the topic is defined as outside the scope of proper inquiry, thus dampening the effect. The positive sign therefore reflects a multiplicative amplification: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. The second-most important interaction, social_science × natural_science, operates at an even more fundamental epistemological level. Its negative sign directly encodes the mutual exclusivity of these two broad domains of knowledge. This is not a trivial statistical artifact but a substantive embodiment of what sociologists of science call "boundary work": the categorical separation between disciplines that study social facts and those that study natural facts. A paper's location in one domain completely rules out the other, and since these domains have diametrically opposed relationships to the topic of racial inequality, their interaction provides a powerful structural constraint on prediction. Without this interaction term, the model would miss the stark, non-linear reality that moving from one disciplinary world to the other is not a matter of degree but of kind. The third interaction, black × authors_race_diversity_score, shifts the analytical lens from the macro-structure of disciplines to the micro-dynamics of collaboration. My reasoning here draws on theories of intergroup contact and collective knowledge production. Team racial diversity alone can be a superficial aggregation without genuine integration of perspectives; a high share of Black authors alone might indicate a team that is relatively homogeneous in its racialized experience. Their positive interaction, however, signals a distinct collaborative configuration: a truly multiracial team where Black scholars are a substantial, non-tokenized presence. I assume that this specific compositional form creates a generative tension within the collaborative process, where the lived reality of racial difference is enacted among co-authors, making the topic of racial inequality not merely an abstract research interest but a salient aspect of the working relationship itself. This reflexive environment, I theorize, is uniquely productive of explicit scholarship on racial inequality, yielding an effect that exceeds the additive contributions of its two constituent features.

Predicting whether a paper discusses racial inequality requires understanding not just who the authors are and where they publish, but when they are writing relative to shifting currents of public and academic discourse, and how disciplinary location conditions responsiveness to those currents. The two most important interactions, social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years, both positive, form the core of this theory. The concept of discursive opportunity structure captures how the scholarly and societal attention environment alters the likelihood of engaging racial inequality, but only for papers in disciplines equipped to capitalize on it. When recent academic literature has paid heightened attention to inequality, a dense, citing, and vital intellectual conversation is underway. Social science papers are positioned to join this conversation because their theoretical frameworks, methodological toolkits, and professional incentive structures are designed to engage social hierarchy as a legitimate object of inquiry. A special issue may have been organized, reviewers may be primed to evaluate inequality manuscripts favorably, and the perceived contribution of an inequality-focused paper is amplified when it can speak to a thriving recent literature. This creates a positive-feedback dynamic: scholarly attention by social scientists begets more scholarly attention by social scientists. Critically, this discursive opportunity structure does not extend across the epistemological boundary into natural science or engineering. A biologist or computer scientist, regardless of personal interest, lacks the disciplinary infrastructure-the relevant theories, the appropriate journals, the receptive peer networks-to join a conversation about racial inequality, even if that conversation is academically vigorous. The positive interaction thus captures the role of social science as the unique institutional site where scholarly momentum toward inequality topics is converted into new published output. A parallel mechanism for the news interaction is societal relevance amplification. When racial inequality surges in public discourse-following catalyzing events, social movements, or political contests-a generalized societal attention to race emerges. This societal energy does not affect all academic production uniformly; it is filtered through disciplinary apparatus. Social scientists are professionally socialized to respond to socially salient problems, and the perceived relevance and fundability of inequality research increases precisely when the public cares most. The societal concern provides both motivation and legitimation, but only social science provides the channel through which this concern can become formal scholarship. The positive interaction thus encodes the institutional translation function of social science: converting societal attention into academic knowledge. The third interaction, female × social_science, with a negative sign, requires a more nuanced theoretical treatment. The simple synergy hypothesis should be rejected in favor of an alternative mechanism grounded in differential baseline constraints. The negative sign indicates that the marginal predictive contribution of female authorship on studying racial inequality diminishes within social science. This occurs not because women in social science are less motivated to study racial inequality, but because of a ceiling effect combined with cross-axis attentional channeling. Social science is already such a powerful positive predictor of racial inequality discourse-the disciplinary current is so strong-that it leaves limited variance for author gender to explain. Within the high-probability environment of social science, additional demographic signals contribute diminishing information. Moreover, the generalized inequality concern associated with female authorship is channeled differently across disciplinary contexts. In social science, where scholars have the full apparatus to study any axis of inequality, women's heightened sensitivity to hierarchy is likely directed toward the axis they experience most directly: gender. The disciplinary richness of social science permits fine-grained specialization, so the female effect manifests within gender-focused subfields rather than spilling over into race. In contrast, women outside social science who possess a generalized inequality concern have fewer legitimate outlets. When they do engage inequality-a rarer event-racial inequality, particularly during periods of high societal salience, may serve as the available and socially visible axis through which this concern is expressed. The negative interaction thus does not imply that social science suppresses female attention to racial inequality, but rather that social science provides the differentiated scholarly channels that allow concern to be directed toward gender specifically, while non-social-science environments compress generalized concern into the few inequality outlets that the broader societal moment makes accessible. This channeling mechanism preserves the underlying assumption that women scholars across disciplines carry a heightened orientation toward social justice, while accounting for the pattern that its disciplinary expression varies by axis. Together, these three interactions structure the theory around a temporal and contextual logic rather than a static compositional one. The likelihood that a paper discusses racial inequality is not merely a function of stable author and discipline characteristics, but of how the disciplinary apparatus-most powerfully social science-interacts with the shifting tides of scholarly conversation and public concern. Author identity features remain important as main effects, but their interactive dynamics are shaped by disciplinary baselines and channeling processes that produce effects more subtle and context-contingent than simple amplification.

My reasoning for the gender inequality task shares the same foundational architecture as my racial inequality model-disciplinary context sets the stage, author positionality provides the motivation and lens-but it diverges in important ways that reflect the distinct social organization of gender as an axis of inequality. At the broadest level, I again place social_science as the most powerful positive predictor. The study of gender inequality, like race, requires engagement with concepts such as power, social structure, and cultural norms that are constitutive of social science disciplines and largely absent from the natural and technical sciences. A paper on patriarchy or sexism is definitionally a social inquiry, and its most fundamental condition of possibility is a disciplinary home that recognizes such inquiry as legitimate scholarship. The second feature, female author share, draws on the same standpoint epistemology that informed my racial inequality predictions. I assume that scholars who directly experience gender-based subordination possess a distinctive epistemic advantage-a combination of visceral knowledge of the phenomenon, personal motivation to understand and challenge it, and heightened sensitivity to its manifestations that others might overlook. The robust overrepresentation of women in gender-focused subfields is not coincidental but reflects these mechanisms operating across countless individual career trajectories. Rounding out the structural constraints, natural_science carries a strong negative sign because its epistemological project is organized around biophysical rather than social explanation, making gender inequality keywords definitionally alien to its scholarly discourse. I elevate engineering_and_technology as a distinct negative predictor for gender because these fields occupy a unique structural position in the gender inequality landscape. They are the frequent objects of gender inequality discourse-as sites of persistent underrepresentation, bias, and "chilly climate" for women-yet this critical conversation predominantly occurs in social science journals about STEM rather than in computer science or engineering journals themselves. This creates a paradox where intense societal attention coexists with a striking absence in the formal academic literature of those fields, sharpening its negative predictive power. Finally, I include authors_race_diversity_score with a positive sign, which may appear unexpected for a gender outcome. My theoretical justification rests on intersectionality and the sociology of intellectual commitments. I assume that scholars engaged in racially diverse collaborations are, on average, more likely to hold broader commitments to equity and social justice that transcend any single axis of inequality. The experience of navigating racial diversity within a team-discussing differing perspectives, acknowledging structural disadvantages-cultivates a reflexive scholarly habitus that lowers the threshold for engaging other forms of inequality, including gender. Additionally, racially diverse teams may simply reflect institutional contexts (e.g., diversity-oriented departments, critical interdisciplinary programs) where attention to multiple forms of hierarchy is normatively expected and professionally rewarded.

A paper's disciplinary home is the most powerful determinant of whether it discusses gender inequality. Social science disciplines—sociology, psychology, political science, gender and women's studies, economics, history—are organized around the systematic investigation of social life, power, and humanly constructed hierarchies. Gender inequality, as a core axis of stratification, is not peripheral but central to these fields' intellectual missions. These disciplines provide the theoretical vocabularies that make gender visible as an object of inquiry—concepts such as patriarchy, sexism, gender performativity, the gender wage gap, and intersectionality—and the professional infrastructure of journals, conferences, and peer networks that legitimate and reward such work. A paper on sex discrimination or gender stereotypes is, definitionally, a social inquiry, and its most fundamental condition of possibility is a disciplinary apparatus that recognizes these phenomena as legitimate scholarly topics. The mirror image is the powerful negative signal carried by natural_science. The natural sciences are organized around biophysical processes that exist independently of human meaning-making—cell division, chemical reactions, planetary motion. Gender inequality, which concerns socially constructed hierarchies, cultural norms, and power relations, falls outside the epistemological boundaries of these disciplines. A biologist or chemist may personally care deeply about gender bias, but the formal scholarly output of their field does not provide a conduit for that concern to manifest in titles and abstracts. Female author share is the central author-identity predictor and the gender analogue to the Black authorship effect for racial inequality. Drawing on standpoint theory and the sociology of knowledge, women scholars, by virtue of their lived experience navigating gender-based subordination—sexism in the workplace, the double bind of likeability and competence, the unequal distribution of domestic labor, the pervasive threat of gender-based violence—possess both heightened personal motivation to understand and challenge these structures and a distinctive epistemic advantage in perceiving their manifestations. This is not an essentialist claim about all women but a structural one about the probabilistic relationship between social location and scholarly attention. The mechanism operates through two reinforcing pathways. The first is motivational: direct experience of gender inequality makes the topic personally salient, fueling the intellectual passion and persistence that sustains research programs. The second is structural sorting: women scholars are disproportionately channeled into gender-focused subfields through mentoring relationships, departmental expectations, and the subtle operation of a scholarly labor market that devalues women's contributions in male-dominated areas while expecting them to carry the burden of diversity-related intellectual work. The association between female authorship and gender inequality research is thus overdetermined by the interplay of individual motivation and institutional channeling. Asian author share extends the framework beyond the simple correspondence model that pairs one identity axis with one inequality axis. Asian authorship may be a general predictor of inequality discourse engagement, not a domain-specific one. This operates through two complementary mechanisms. The first mechanism concerns the internationalization and global diversification of inequality research. Scholars from and in Asian societies—including India, China, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and others—are contributing to a rapidly growing global literature on gender inequality that examines non-Western contexts. These societies feature salient and often distinctive forms of gender hierarchy: patrilineal kinship structures, pronounced son preference and sex-selective practices, rapidly changing but persistent gender gaps in labor force participation, and dynamic feminist movements that have emerged in dialogue with but distinct from Western feminisms. This empirical richness provides fertile ground for gender inequality scholarship, and the increasing internationalization of academic publishing has made this work more visible in the English-language scholarly corpus. The second mechanism concerns the diaspora and comparative perspective. Asian scholars working in Western academic institutions—as graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and faculty—often navigate multiple cultural frameworks, experiencing the contrast between gender arrangements in their countries of origin and their host societies. This bicultural or multicultural positioning can generate a distinctive scholarly attunement to the constructedness and variability of gender, making it more likely to be problematized and studied rather than taken for granted as natural. This comparative sensibility is a cognitive resource that translates into heightened engagement with gender inequality as a scholarly topic. Paper_inequality_mentions_3_years introduces a temporal dimension through the concept of discursive momentum within the academic field. Scholarship does not proceed in isolation but within a dynamic intellectual environment where the recent density of attention to a topic alters the conditions for new contributions. When the recent academic literature has paid heightened attention to inequality, a thriving intellectual conversation is underway, generating several self-reinforcing dynamics. Theoretical frameworks are being refined and contested, creating openings for new contributions that extend, critique, or synthesize. Reviewers are primed to evaluate inequality manuscripts as timely and relevant. Special issues and edited volumes may be in development, creating concrete publication opportunities. The perceived importance and citability of inequality research rises, making it professionally rewarding. This discursive momentum operates across axes of inequality; the measure captures general inequality attention, and its spillover effect means that when race and class inequality are also ascendant in the scholarly conversation, gender inequality research benefits from the broader intellectual energy around social justice. Temporal attention cycles are not noise around a stable baseline but a constitutive feature of how academic knowledge production operates: the likelihood of a paper engaging gender inequality depends not only on who writes it and where, but on when it enters the scholarly conversation relative to these shifting currents of collective attention. Engineering_and_technology may have a negative association, but that signal is largely captured by natural_science; the additional discriminatory power of distinguishing engineering from natural science is modest. Authors_race_diversity_score may reflect a cross-axis solidarity mechanism at the margins, but it is weaker than the more direct pathways of disciplinary location, author gender identity, international scholarly positioning, and temporal attention cycles. The theory therefore centers discipline as gatekeeper and author positionality as motivator, while also incorporating temporal scholarly attention cycles and Asian authorship as cross-cutting predictors of engagement with gender inequality.

My selection of these three interactions is organized around a core theoretical principle: the expression of author positionality is always contingent on the disciplinary context in which scholarship is produced, and the most analytically powerful interactions are those that capture how institutional structures either amplify or suppress the scholarly potential of lived experience. The most important interaction, social_science × female, embodies what I theorize as the essential synergy between experiential motivation and disciplinary opportunity. My foundational assumption is that while women scholars, on average, possess a heightened personal stake in understanding and challenging gender inequality due to their direct encounters with sexism, patriarchal norms, and structural disadvantage, this motivation alone is insufficient to produce published research on the topic. It requires a disciplinary home that recognizes gender as a legitimate category of scholarly inquiry, provides theoretical frameworks such as feminist theory or gender studies, and offers professional rewards for such work through sympathetic reviewers, dedicated journals, and receptive collegial networks. Social science disciplines furnish precisely this scaffolding, creating what I call an "amplification zone" where personal motivation is institutionally channeled and legitimated. The positive sign of this interaction thus captures a multiplicative rather than merely additive effect: a woman in sociology does not simply carry two independent positive predictors but operates in a context where her standpoint-derived insights are actively cultivated. The second-most important interaction, social_science × natural_science, operates at a deeper structural level that I term the epistemological divide. Its negative sign encodes the hard boundary between two incommensurable modes of knowledge production. I assume that academic disciplines are not merely different in degree but fundamentally different in kind when it comes to their object of study-social sciences are organized around understanding socially constructed realities, while natural sciences focus on biophysical processes that exist independently of human meaning-making. A paper's location in one domain categorically precludes the other, and since these domains have antithetical relationships to gender as a topic of formal inquiry, the interaction provides a powerful structural constraint that a purely additive model would miss. This is not a statistical nuance but a substantive representation of what sociologists of science recognize as the foundational boundary work that constitutes modern disciplines. The third interaction, female × natural_science, shifts the analytical focus to what I theorize as a mechanism of structural suppression. My reasoning here draws on a rich body of research on the position of women in male-dominated STEM fields, which documents a paradoxical dynamic. Women in these disciplines disproportionately experience the very phenomena-bias, exclusion, chilly climate-that constitute gender inequality, yet they face strong countervailing pressures that inhibit them from making these experiences the object of their formal scholarly work. I assume that these pressures operate through multiple channels: professional socialization that defines gender-focused research as less rigorous or central, strategic career concerns that discourage being pigeonholed as "the woman who studies women," and the simple absence of mentors, reviewers, and departmental colleagues who would validate such inquiry. The negative sign of this interaction captures this dampening effect, where the motivation associated with female identity is actively suppressed rather than merely unrewarded, creating a silence that is especially pronounced given the heightened personal relevance of the topic. Together, these three interactions form a coherent theoretical architecture: the first identifies where standpoint-driven scholarship flourishes, the second demarcates the categorical boundary that constrains all social inquiry, and the third reveals where structural forces actively silence the very voices whose experience would otherwise propel attention to gender inequality.

The interactions social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years, both positive, form the temporal core of this theory and are general mechanisms that operate across inequality domains. I theorize these through the concept of discursive opportunity structure, which captures how the broader scholarly and societal attention environment alters the likelihood of engaging inequality, but only for papers in disciplines equipped to capitalize on that environment. When recent academic literature has paid heightened attention to inequality—whether racial, gender, or economic—a dense, citing, and intellectually vital conversation is underway. This creates receptive conditions: reviewers are familiar with and favorably disposed toward inequality frameworks, special issues and edited volumes provide concrete publication venues, and the perceived importance of inequality scholarship is elevated. Social science papers are uniquely positioned to join and extend this conversation because they possess the theoretical vocabularies, methodological toolkits, and professional incentive structures that make inequality a legitimate object of inquiry. A paper in natural science or engineering, regardless of its authors' personal interests, lacks the disciplinary infrastructure to enter this conversation; the discursive opportunity structure does not extend across the epistemological boundary. The parallel mechanism for news attention operates through societal relevance amplification. When inequality surges in public discourse—whether through social movements like #MeToo, political controversies over equal pay, or catalyzing events that draw attention to gender-based violence—a generalized societal concern with gender hierarchy emerges. This societal energy does not affect all academic fields uniformly; it is filtered through disciplinary apparatus. Social scientists are professionally socialized to respond to problems of public concern, and the perceived relevance and fundability of gender inequality research increases precisely when the public cares most. Social science thus serves as the institutional translator that converts societal attention into formal scholarly knowledge. The positive interaction for academic attention and the positive interaction for news attention represent, respectively, the internal and external faces of this translational function: social science amplifies the effects of both scholarly momentum and public concern. The female × social_science interaction, with a negative sign, is best understood through three complementary mechanisms, which together form a differential diagnosticity framework. The first and most important mechanism is a ceiling effect. Social science is such a powerful positive predictor of gender inequality discourse that the baseline probability within this disciplinary context is already very high. When a social science paper is already highly likely to discuss gender inequality regardless of author demographics, the marginal predictive contribution of any additional feature—including female authorship—is necessarily compressed. The female effect can only operate where there is variance to explain, and social science leaves little room for it. The second mechanism concerns baseline diagnosticity outside social science. In natural science, engineering, and other non-social-science fields, studying gender inequality is a rare, counter-normative act that deviates from the dominant intellectual agenda of the discipline. When a paper in these fields does engage gender inequality, author gender becomes a highly informative signal because it helps explain the deviation. A woman in a male-dominated engineering department writing about sexism in STEM is likely doing so precisely because her personal experience in that context makes the topic urgent and unavoidable; her authorship is deeply diagnostic of the paper's content in a way that a female sociologist's authorship is not, because the latter is simply doing what many scholars—men and women alike—do in her field. The third mechanism introduces a dynamic of within-discipline heterogeneity and strategic self-presentation outside social science. In non-social-science fields, where studying gender is unusual and may carry professional risk, the women who do so are a self-selected group with particularly strong motivation. This selection effect tightens the female-gender inequality link precisely where the baseline is lowest. Meanwhile, within social science, many male scholars study gender inequality as a legitimate and even prestigious specialization, further eroding the gender diagnosticity of the topic within that disciplinary context. The negative interaction thus does not imply that social science suppresses female engagement with gender inequality—the main effect of female remains positive overall—but rather that the predictive value of knowing an author's gender is greatest in the disciplinary contexts where gender inequality scholarship is scarcest and therefore most informative as a signal of authorial motivation. Together, these three interactions structure the theory around a logic that is simultaneously temporal and differential. The likelihood that a paper discusses gender inequality depends not only on stable features of discipline and authorship but on when the paper enters the scholarly conversation relative to shifting currents of academic and public attention, and on how the diagnosticity of author identity varies inversely with the disciplinary baseline. This framework preserves the core insight that female authorship is a robust positive predictor of gender inequality discourse, while explaining why its marginal predictive power is greatest not where such discourse is most common, but where it is most unexpected.

My ranking rests on the premise that whether a paper discusses racial inequality is determined jointly by disciplinary opportunity, temporal salience, and author standpoint, in roughly that order of force. Disciplinary scope comes first because the inequality keywords are essentially the working vocabulary of the social sciences; a journal's scope sets the boundary conditions for whether such language can plausibly appear at all, which is why social_science carries the strongest positive sign and engineering_and_technology the clearest negative one (with only a modest weakening from the recent rise of algorithmic-fairness work that imports "racial bias" into computer science). I rank the two contextual trend variables highly because the production of academic knowledge is not insulated from its environment: paper_inequality_mentions_3_years captures intellectual momentum and agenda-setting within the field—rising attention makes the topic more citable, fundable, and legitimate—while news_inequality_mentions_3_years captures the broader public attention cycle that spills into scholarly agendas with a short lag (e.g., surges around high-profile racial-justice events). I place the within-academia signal above the news signal on the assumption that scholars respond more directly to their own field's conversation than to media coverage. The inclusion of black with a positive sign reflects a standpoint-and-homophily logic: scholars whose own group experiences racial marginalization are disproportionately motivated to study it, so author identity proxies for topical self-selection. The key assumptions underlying all of this are that journal scope reliably constrains topical content, that attention to inequality diffuses across the news–academy boundary, and that the name-and-country-based identity inferences—though noisy—are accurate enough in aggregate to preserve the true direction of the standpoint effect.

Whether a paper discusses racial inequality is governed by three forces—disciplinary opportunity, author standpoint broadly construed, and temporal salience. Disciplinary scope remains the master variable and strongest predictor: the racial-inequality lexicon is the native vocabulary of the social sciences, so social_science is the dominant positive driver and engineering/natural-science scope suppresses the topic by denying it vocabulary, venues, and legitimacy. Author composition matters through a broader, two-part standpoint account rather than only through own-group membership. First, there is a general equity-disposition channel: women, regardless of race, are disproportionately drawn to inequality scholarship of all kinds, partly as a dispositional orientation and partly because the equity-oriented subfields that house racial-inequality work are themselves female-dominated, so female authorship proxies both a disposition and a sub-disciplinary location that a coarse social_science binary fails to capture. Second, there is an exposure-to-racial-difference channel that supplements—rather than replaces—own-group standpoint: authors from racially diverse countries and Asian authors, often internationally mobile and themselves racialized within host academic systems, acquire heightened salience of race through lived heterogeneity, so racial topics become salient not only to those who belong to a marginalized group but to those exposed to racial difference generally; this is why diversity and Asian share, alongside Black share, all carry positive signs. Finally, temporal/contextual variables such as paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and news_inequality_mentions_3_years matter causally in an absolute sense—rising societal and intra-academic attention genuinely lifts the volume of racial-inequality work—but they are weak cross-sectional discriminators because they vary little across papers within a given time window, so a feature can be causally real yet uninformative for classifying one paper against another. The core assumptions are that journal scope constrains topical content; that author composition matters through a broadened standpoint logic combining general equity-disposition, exposure to racial difference, and own-group membership; and that slow-moving attention cycles are causally relevant but empirically low-variance predictors at the paper level.

My three interactions share a common logic: the effect of any single driver of racial-inequality discourse is conditional on whether the structural opportunity to express that discourse exists, and disciplinary scope is the master conditioning variable. The strongest interaction, social_science × black, reflects my assumption that author standpoint cannot operate in a vacuum—a Black scholar's heightened motivation to study racial marginalization only converts into a keyword-bearing paper when situated in a field whose journals, vocabulary, and reviewers treat racial inequality as legitimate subject matter; in engineering or natural-science venues that same motivation has little outlet, so the two forces are multiplicative rather than merely additive, yielding a positive sign. The second interaction, social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years, rests on the same conditionality applied to temporal salience: a rising tide of inequality attention across the literature can only lift papers in disciplines positioned to absorb it, so field-wide momentum and disciplinary fit reinforce one another positively, while the trend is largely inert in technical fields. The third, black × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years, captures a within-person amplification: when the broader field signals that inequality is timely, legitimate, and fundable, the latent standpoint motivation of Black authors is further activated and de-risked, so identity and temporal opportunity compound positively. The unifying assumption is one of complementarity—motivation, attention, and disciplinary opportunity are inputs that multiply rather than substitute, so each becomes most powerful precisely when the others are also present.

A theory of second-order interactions distinguishes between two structurally different ways features combine—complementarity and substitution. The dominant pattern is complementarity between temporal attention and disciplinary opportunity: social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years are both strongly positive because rising attention to inequality, whether originating inside academia or in the public sphere, can only convert into actual racial-inequality papers within disciplines that possess the vocabulary, venues, and legitimacy to absorb it. Neither input is sufficient alone—a salience surge is inert in technical fields, and disciplinary fit needs an activating climate—so they multiply. This interactive structure also explains why temporal variables can have weak standalone discriminating power: their causal force is conditional, expressed only through interaction with discipline, so they surface as important interaction terms even while being weak main effects. For standpoint × discipline, there is a substitution rather than complementarity logic for variables that proxy disciplinary location. The female × social_science interaction is negative because female authorship partly stands in for being situated in equity-oriented, female-dominated subfields; once a paper is already identified as social science, that proxy becomes largely redundant, so female authorship's marginal informational contribution is largest outside social science, where a female-authored technical paper is a rare and strong signal of a deliberate turn toward inequality themes. The two variables are therefore substitutes at the margin—each most diagnostic when the other is absent—driven by informational overlap and ceiling effects. The unifying assumption is that whether an interaction is positive or negative depends on the informational relationship between the two features: when they capture distinct, jointly necessary inputs, such as attention and opportunity, they complement and the sign is positive; when one feature is partly a proxy for the other, such as female authorship for equity-subfield location, which discipline already encodes, they substitute and the sign is negative. Genuine own-group or exposure-based standpoint variables, such as Black share, Asian share, and country diversity, are expected to interact positively with discipline, but this prediction is more tentative because any standpoint variable carrying a sub-disciplinary-location component may instead substitute for the social_science indicator.

My ranking again assumes that whether a paper discusses gender inequality is governed jointly by disciplinary opportunity, author standpoint, and temporal salience, but with the standpoint channel elevated relative to the racial task. Disciplinary scope leads because the gender-inequality lexicon—patriarchy, sexism, sex discrimination, gender stereotypes—is the native working vocabulary of the social sciences, so social_science is the strongest positive predictor and engineering_and_technology the clearest negative one (weakened only modestly by the recent influx of "gender bias" fairness work and "women in STEM" research into technical fields). I place female second, above the contextual trend variables, because gender is the most directly self-relevant identity axis available in this feature set: under standpoint and homophily logic, women are disproportionately motivated to study gender as a subject, and unlike the name-and-country-inferred racial shares, the name-based gender inference is comparatively accurate, so the signal is both theoretically strong and well-measured—hence a robust positive sign. The two attention variables follow: paper_inequality_mentions_3_years captures intra-academic momentum that raises the legitimacy and fundability of gender work, and news_inequality_mentions_3_years captures the broader public attention cycle—episodic surges around events like #MeToo—that diffuses into scholarly agendas with a short lag, with the within-field signal ranked above the media signal on the assumption that scholars respond most directly to their own field's conversation. The core assumptions are that journal scope constrains topical content, that gendered self-relevance drives topic self-selection more strongly than any other identity axis here, and that attention to inequality crosses the news–academy boundary in a predictable, lagged fashion.

Whether a paper discusses gender inequality is governed by disciplinary opportunity, author composition, and temporal salience. Disciplinary scope remains the master variable: the gender-inequality lexicon (patriarchy, sexism, sex discrimination, gender stereotypes) is the native vocabulary of the social sciences, so social_science is the dominant positive driver, while non-social fields suppress the topic by denying it vocabulary, venues, and legitimacy. The strongest exclusionary signal is natural_science rather than engineering_and_technology; both suppress the topic in mechanism, but natural science is likely the largest disciplinary block in the corpus and therefore carries more cross-sectional discriminating power, making natural_science the principal negative discipline while engineering is secondarily exclusionary. On author composition, female_score is the second-strongest predictor, consistent with the core claim that gender is the most self-relevant identity axis and that women are disproportionately motivated to study gender—reinforced by the fact that name-based gender inference is comparatively accurate, making this both a theoretically strong and well-measured signal. Author-composition variables also tap a broad orientation toward inequality scholarship of all forms rather than strictly matching the inequality type to the author's own group. Under this generalized equity-disposition account, female authorship reflects both a genuine gender-specific standpoint and a general equity-disposition (and partly a location in equity-oriented, female-dominated subfields), while Asian authorship—likely capturing internationally mobile authors with heightened salience of social hierarchy and exposure to difference—contributes a generalized sensitivity to inequality that spills across the racial/gender boundary. The temporal channel also matters: paper_inequality_mentions_3_years carries genuine intra-academic momentum and shows more standalone discriminating power for gender than for race—plausibly because gender-inequality discourse expanded especially steadily over 2000–2020, giving the trend more within-sample variance—whereas news_inequality_mentions remains causally relevant but a weak paper-level discriminator because slow-moving aggregate attention varies little across papers within a window. The core assumptions are that journal scope constrains topical content (with natural science the dominant suppressor); that author composition operates through a broadened logic combining gender-specific standpoint (female), general equity-disposition, and exposure-to-difference (Asian, mobility); and that intra-academic attention matters more than public attention at the paper level, with both causally real but differing in cross-sectional variance.

My three interactions follow a single principle of complementarity: the drivers of gender-inequality discourse multiply rather than substitute, and disciplinary scope is the master conditioning variable that determines whether any other force can be expressed. The strongest interaction, social_science × female, rests on the assumption that author standpoint cannot operate without structural opportunity—a female scholar's heightened motivation to study gender only converts into a keyword-bearing paper when situated in a field whose journals, vocabulary, and reviewers treat gender inequality as legitimate subject matter; in technical or natural-science venues that same motivation has little outlet, so the two forces compound multiplicatively and the sign is positive. I place this above the others because gender is the most directly self-relevant identity axis and the female share is comparatively well-measured, making the interaction both theoretically potent and empirically clean. The second interaction, social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years, applies the same conditionality to temporal salience: a rising tide of inequality attention across the literature can only lift papers in disciplines positioned to absorb it, so field-wide momentum and disciplinary fit reinforce one another positively while remaining largely inert in technical fields. The third, female × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years, captures within-person amplification: when the broader field signals that inequality work is timely, legitimate, and fundable, the latent standpoint motivation of women authors is further activated and de-risked, so identity and temporal opportunity compound positively. The unifying assumption throughout is that motivation, attention, and disciplinary opportunity are complementary inputs—each becomes most powerful precisely when the others are also present.

A theory of second-order interactions for gender inequality distinguishes two ways features combine—complementarity and substitution—rather than assuming uniform multiplicative amplification. The dominant pattern is complementarity between temporal attention and disciplinary opportunity: social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years are both strongly positive because attention to inequality, whether originating inside academia or in the public sphere, can only convert into actual gender-inequality papers within disciplines that possess the vocabulary, venues, and legitimacy to absorb it. Neither input is sufficient alone—a salience surge is inert in technical or natural-science fields, and disciplinary fit needs an activating climate—so they multiply, and this interactive structure explains why the temporal variables can surface as strong interactions even when their standalone discriminating power is only modest: their causal force is conditional, expressed through discipline. Standpoint × discipline follows a substitution rather than complementarity logic. The female × social_science interaction is negative because female authorship partly proxies location in equity-oriented, female-dominated subfields; once a paper is already identified as social science, that proxy becomes largely redundant, so female authorship's marginal informational contribution is largest outside social science, where a female-authored natural-science or technical paper is a rare and strong signal of a deliberate turn toward gender themes. This substitution—driven by informational overlap and ceiling effects—is especially notable for the gender task because gender is the most self-relevant axis and female_score is well-measured. The unifying assumption is that the sign of an interaction depends on the informational relationship between the two features: when they capture distinct, jointly necessary inputs (attention and disciplinary opportunity), they complement and the sign is positive; when one feature is partly a proxy for what the other already encodes (female authorship for equity-subfield location, which discipline captures), they substitute and the sign is negative. The more general principle is that any author-composition variable carrying a sub-disciplinary-location component will tend to substitute for, rather than amplify, the disciplinary indicator.

My rankings rest on a layered model in which opportunity, motivation, and temporal climate jointly determine whether a paper invokes racial-inequality language. The top tier reflects disciplinary jurisdiction: scholarly fields are institutionalized "ecologies" with their own legitimate objects of study, vocabularies, and reward structures, and racial inequality is a core, fundable, publishable object in the social sciences but largely outside the epistemic mandate of engineering and the natural sciences. This is why `social_science` (+) ranks first and `engineering_and_technology` (−) ranks third — they are essentially the positive and negative poles of the same structural sorting mechanism, with the negative pole slightly weaker because computer science's recent "algorithmic fairness/bias" turn smuggles some keyword hits back in. The second-ranked feature, `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), and the fifth, `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), capture discursive opportunity structure over time: attention to inequality moves in waves driven by social movements and events (e.g., Black Lives Matter, 2020), and a rising ambient salience lowers the cost and raises the payoff of framing one's work in inequality terms, producing a bandwagon/agenda-setting dynamic. I rank the scholarly proxy above the news proxy because academic citation and topic cascades are the more proximate channel through which a given author decides what is "current" and citable, with media salience operating one step upstream. The placement of `black` (+) at fourth reflects a standpoint and homophily mechanism: scholars' own social positions shape the questions they find salient and urgent, so author teams with higher inferred Black representation are disproportionately likely to study racial inequality — but I rank it below the structural and temporal features, and treat its sign with caution, because the measure is constructed by imputing individual race from last-name-to-country-to-national-racial-composition, a pipeline that injects substantial measurement error and almost certainly attenuates the true association. Underlying all of this are two assumptions: first, that the keyword-based label primarily captures explicit topical framing rather than latent substance, so features predicting the choice to name inequality (field norms, temporal fashion, authorial standpoint) matter more than features predicting underlying content; and second, that the strongest and most stable signals come from structural/contextual variables that are measured well (field, time-trend) rather than from demographic variables that are measured noisily.

The theory rests on a structural foundation organized around three layers and around a distinction between forces that explain the longitudinal rate of racial-inequality discourse and forces that discriminate among contemporaneous papers. The first layer is disciplinary jurisdiction: fields are institutionalized epistemic ecologies with their own legitimate objects, vocabularies, journals, and reward structures, and racial inequality is a core, fundable, publishable object in the social sciences but largely outside the mandate of engineering and the natural sciences. This is why `social_science` (+) is the strongest predictor, and why `engineering_and_technology` (−) remains its negative pole: field membership is the master sorting variable. The second layer treats author identity, standpoint, and societal exposure as the primary engine of paper-level variation, not a secondary noisy channel. Who writes the paper is what separates a racial-inequality paper from its same-year, same-field neighbors.
