This is not a single "Black-scholar standpoint" path but a broader latent construct, an "inequality-oriented author profile," generated by several distinct sub-mechanisms: (a) an intersectional / general social-justice orientation that explains the `female_score` (+) effect — women in academia are overrepresented in inequality-attuned subfields and questions, so female authorship proxies a disposition to study social disadvantage across axes, including race, rather than gender alone; (b) a societal-exposure mechanism behind `country_race_diversity_score` (+) — scholars from racially heterogeneous societies (above all the United States, also Brazil and South Africa) experience race as a salient social fact and dominate the production of racial-inequality scholarship, so exposure operates at the level of the author's social context, not just team composition; and (c) a minority-representation / standpoint mechanism behind `black` (+) and `asian` (+), where members of racially marked groups, and teams situated in diverse academic settings, are disproportionately motivated to name and study racial inequality — with the caveat that `asian` may partly co-travel with country diversity and warrants a controlled test. The persistence of these demographic effects despite the heavy measurement error in the race-imputation pipeline suggests that the underlying standpoint/exposure signal is strong. The third layer is temporal/discursive climate: `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` almost certainly govern the aggregate rise of racial-inequality discourse over time (e.g., the post-2013 and 2020 surges), but because ambient salience is shared by nearly all papers in a given window — most of which still do not discuss race — these variables have little power to classify individual papers. The two assumptions anchoring the theory are: first, that the keyword label captures explicit topical framing, so the decision to name race is driven jointly by field permission and authorial disposition; and second, that feature importance in this task reflects cross-sectional separation, which rewards paper-varying identity and field variables over time-varying contextual ones, elevating author identity to the center of the explanation.

All three interactions share one underlying logic: disciplinary membership is the gatekeeping condition that allows other forces to express themselves as racial-inequality discourse. I treat `social_science` not merely as an additive booster but as a moderating context — an enabling ecology with the vocabulary, theoretical traditions, journals, reviewers, and reward structures that make naming racial inequality both legitimate and publishable. Outside that ecology (e.g., in engineering or the natural sciences), the same impulses have no sanctioned outlet, so their slopes flatten toward zero. This is why every interaction I selected is positive and why each pairs `social_science` with a force whose effect I believe is latent until a field activates it. For the first and most important interaction, `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), my assumption is that the temporal "salience wave" of inequality attention does not lift all fields equally: when ambient scholarly attention to inequality rises (e.g., after 2013 and especially 2020), social scientists are positioned to ride that wave — reframing projects, launching new ones, and citing the moment — whereas a chemistry or mechanical-engineering paper is largely insulated from it, so the wave's predictive power is concentrated where the mandate exists. The third interaction, `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), is the same mechanism operating one step upstream through the public sphere: media-driven salience translates into academic framing chiefly among scholars whose discipline treats public social problems as legitimate objects, so media climate matters far more for social-science output than for technical fields. The second interaction, `social_science × black` (+), reflects a standpoint-times-opportunity logic: a scholar's social position may generate motivation and lived urgency to study racial inequality, but motivation converts into a published, keyword-bearing paper only where the field affords the topic — so the standpoint effect of Black author share is amplified inside social science and muted where the discipline offers no path to publish such work. The governing assumption across all three is multiplicative gating rather than simple addition: temporal climate, public attention, and authorial standpoint are best understood as potentials whose realization is conditional on a permissive disciplinary environment, which is why the interaction terms carry real, positive explanatory weight beyond the main effects.

A theory of interactions should abandon a single, uniform logic in which "the discipline amplifies everything" and instead use a two-logic framework distinguished by the nature of the interacting input. The organizing idea is that `social_science` functions as the master contextual moderator, but whether it amplifies or dampens another feature depends on whether that feature is a complement to the field's mandate or a substitute for it. The first logic is complementarity / super-additivity, which governs contextual-temporal inputs: the salience wave captured by `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` cannot raise an individual paper's probability of discussing race on its own — ambient attention is shared by nearly all papers in a given window and is inert as a main effect — but it becomes potent precisely when it meets a field equipped to act on it. Social scientists are positioned to ride a rising tide of inequality attention, reframing projects, launching new ones, and citing the moment, whereas technical fields are insulated, so the marginal effect of the wave is concentrated inside social science and the product terms `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` are strongly positive. The temporal climate matters predictively only in interaction with field, even when temporal main effects are weak. The second logic is substitution / saturation / sub-additivity, which governs author-identity inputs. Both being in social science and having a high female author share are partially redundant routes to the same outcome — each independently pushes a paper toward inequality framing — so when one route is already active the other adds less. Inside social science the legitimacy to discuss race is already near a ceiling, making the response surface concave, so additional female authorship yields diminishing marginal returns; conversely, outside social science female authorship becomes highly diagnostic, flagging the specific subset of medical, educational, or STEM-adjacent papers oriented toward diversity and disparities, where it is one of the few signals that a paper will invoke racial-diversity or racial-bias language. The result is that the female effect is largest where the field's mandate is weakest, producing a negative `female × social_science` interaction. `social_science × black` is not expected to be a leading interaction: the `black` main effect is weak and heavily attenuated by the race-imputation pipeline, so its interaction is too noisy to surface, and in any case the demographic-standpoint channel that does surface (`female`) operates by substitution rather than amplification. The cross-axis appearance of `female` in a racial-inequality model reflects a general "inequality-oriented author" disposition that travels across fields, which is exactly why it acts as a substitute for the field's own mandate rather than as a within-field amplifier. The governing assumption is therefore that interaction sign is determined by whether a feature complements or substitutes for disciplinary legitimacy: contextual/temporal forces are complements, producing positive interactions because they require the field to be activated, whereas portable author-identity dispositions are substitutes, producing negative interactions because they can supply inequality orientation even where the field does not.

My gender rankings follow the same three-layer logic I applied to race — disciplinary jurisdiction, temporal climate, and authorial standpoint — but with one consequential reordering driven by measurement quality. As before, disciplinary mandate anchors the top: `social_science` (+) ranks first and `engineering_and_technology` (−) fourth because fields are institutionalized epistemic ecologies, and gender inequality is a central, theorized, publishable object in sociology, psychology, and the humanities while sitting largely outside the legitimate problem-space of technical fields. The crucial departure from the racial task is that author standpoint moves up to second place: I rank `female` (+) above the temporal-salience features, whereas I placed `black` only fourth in the racial model. The substantive mechanism is the same — homophily and lived experience make members of a disadvantaged group disproportionately likely to study that group's disadvantage, and gender scholarship (feminist theory, sex-discrimination research, gender-stereotype work) is unusually female-authored — but the reason for the higher rank is methodological as much as theoretical: gender is inferred from first names, which is a reasonably accurate signal, so the `female` variable carries far less attenuation bias than the noisy race-imputation pipeline that crippled `black`. In other words, I believe the true standpoint effect is strong in both cases, but only in the gender task is it measured well enough to surface as a top predictor. The two temporal features, `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+, rank 3) and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+, rank 5), capture the discursive opportunity structure over time — gender-equality attention moves in event-driven waves (notably #MeToo from 2017) that lower the cost and raise the payoff of framing work in gender terms — and I again place the scholarly proxy above the media proxy because intra-academic topic cascades are the more proximate channel governing what an author treats as current and citable, with media salience operating one step upstream. Two assumptions underlie the whole ordering: first, that the keyword label captures explicit topical framing rather than latent content, so features predicting the decision to name gender inequality (field norms, authorial standpoint, temporal fashion) dominate; and second, that observed feature importance reflects true effect size × measurement reliability, which is precisely why a well-measured demographic variable (`female`) outranks the temporal proxies here even though a poorly-measured one (`black`) did not in the racial model.

My gender theory retains a three-layer architecture — disciplinary jurisdiction, author identity, and temporal climate — with disciplinary jurisdiction as the master sorter. `social_science` (+) is the strongest predictor because fields are institutionalized epistemic ecologies and gender inequality is a central, theorized, fundable, publishable object there. The negative pole is outcome-specific rather than a fixed "technical fields are negative" rule. For gender, the suppressor is `natural_science` (−), not engineering, because engineering and computer science host their own vigorous gender-equity discourse — women-in-STEM, diversity in engineering, gender bias in AI — which lifts those fields toward the keyword set and leaves the natural sciences (biology, chemistry, physics, much of medicine), where "patriarchy/sexism/gender-stereotype" language rarely appears, as the cleaner negative pole. Disciplinary effects are the joint product of a field's general mandate to study social problems and its topic-specific internal discourse, the latter of which can partially rehabilitate an otherwise "technical" field for one inequality axis (gender) but not another (race). The second layer, author identity / standpoint, is the primary paper-level engine: `female_score` (+) ranks second because the gender-standpoint mechanism is both substantively powerful (homophily and lived salience make female-authored teams disproportionately likely to study gender inequality) and, crucially, well-measured (first-name gender inference is accurate), so unlike the attenuated `black` effect in the racial model it surfaces near the top rather than being buried by measurement noise. `asian` (+) appears as a general, portable "inequality-oriented / diverse-context author" signal — authors situated in racially heterogeneous, frequently US-based, social-science-adjacent environments where inequality of all kinds is salient — rather than as an axis-specific standpoint, which is the same broad disposition that explains why `female` predicts racial inequality too. In other words, the second layer is best understood as a set of partly overlapping channels feeding one latent construct, an inequality-oriented author profile, that travels across axes rather than a collection of strictly axis-matched standpoints. The third layer, temporal/discursive climate, remains demoted but with a nuance: `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) edges into the main-effect top five for gender, whereas the temporal variables dropped out entirely for race. I attribute this to the shape of the salience shock: the gender wave has a sharper, later jump within the 2000–2020 window (#MeToo, 2017) than the more gradual racial build-up, giving the lagged-mention variable steeper within-sample variance and thus modestly more paper-level discriminating power; `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` again fails to surface, consistent with media climate being the most-shared, least-discriminating, most upstream contextual variable. The governing assumptions of the theory are: first, that the keyword label captures explicit framing, so the decision to name gender inequality is driven jointly by field permission and a portable authorial disposition; second, that observed importance reflects true effect size × measurement reliability, which is why a well-measured standpoint variable (`female`) leads here while a poorly-measured one (`black`) did not in the racial model; and third, that disciplinary and temporal effects are outcome-specific in form — the negative field depends on which axis has homegrown disciplinary discourse, and temporal climate discriminates at the paper level only to the extent its salience shock is sharp.

These three interactions rest on the same governing principle I used for race — disciplinary membership is the enabling condition that converts latent forces into actual gender-inequality discourse — but the ordering shifts to reflect what I believe is an unusually strong, and unusually well-measured, standpoint effect. I treat `social_science` as a moderator, an ecology supplying the vocabulary, theoretical traditions, journals, and reviewers that make naming gender inequality legitimate and publishable; outside it, the same impulses lack a sanctioned outlet and their slopes flatten toward zero. This multiplicative-gating logic is why all three interactions are positive. The first and most important, `social_science × female` (+), encodes a standpoint-times-opportunity mechanism: female author share generates motivation and lived salience to study gender inequality, but that motivation becomes a published, keyword-bearing paper chiefly where the discipline affords the topic, so the female effect is amplified inside social science and muted in technical fields. I elevate this above the temporal interactions — reversing the priority I gave the analogous `social_science × black` term in the racial model — for two reasons: substantively, gender homophily in feminist and gender scholarship is especially strong, and methodologically, first-name gender inference is accurate enough that the interaction is not washed out by measurement error the way the noisy race imputation was. The second and third interactions, `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) and `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), capture the temporal salience wave operating through a disciplinary filter: event-driven surges in attention to gender inequality (most clearly #MeToo from 2017) do not lift all fields equally, because only scholars whose discipline treats public gender problems as legitimate objects are positioned to ride the wave — reframing, launching, and citing the moment — while a technical paper remains largely insulated. I again rank the scholarly proxy above the media proxy because intra-academic topic cascades are the more proximate channel through which authors register what is "current," with media salience acting one step upstream. The core assumption throughout is that authorial standpoint, scholarly fashion, and public attention are potentials whose realization is conditional on a permissive field, so their explanatory power surfaces in the interaction terms rather than in main effects alone — and that, between the two demographic standpoints, the gender one rises to the top of the interaction ranking precisely because it is the one we can measure cleanly.

A theory of gender interactions follows the same two-logic framework as for race, as a domain-general principle. The organizing idea is that `social_science` acts as the master contextual moderator, but whether it amplifies or dampens another feature depends entirely on whether that feature is a complement to the field's mandate or a substitute for it. The first logic, complementarity / super-additivity, governs contextual–temporal inputs: the ambient salience captured by `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` cannot lift an individual paper's probability of discussing gender on its own — it is shared by nearly all papers in a given window and is largely inert as a main effect — but it becomes potent precisely when it meets a field equipped to act on it. Social scientists are positioned to ride a rising tide of inequality attention, reframing projects, launching new ones, citing the moment, e.g., around #MeToo, whereas other fields are insulated, so the wave's marginal effect concentrates inside social science and the product terms `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) and `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) are strongly positive and top the interaction ranking, as in the racial model. This also resolves an apparent tension with the main-effects pattern: temporal climate is weak or borderline as a main effect yet leads the interaction ranking, because its predictive power is conditional on disciplinary activation rather than freestanding. The second logic, substitution / saturation / sub-additivity, governs author-identity inputs. Both being in social science and having a high female author share independently push a paper toward gender-inequality framing, so they are partially redundant routes to the same outcome; when one route is already active the other adds less. Inside social science, gender inequality is discussed near a ceiling regardless of author gender, making the response surface concave and giving additional female authorship diminishing returns; outside social science, a female-heavy team is highly diagnostic, flagging the specific subset of women-in-STEM, female-authored medical, or engineering-education papers that invoke gender-inequality language, so the female effect is largest exactly where the field mandate is weakest. The result is a negative `female × social_science` interaction. This substitution logic is not an artifact of measurement error: in the racial model the pattern could partly be attributed to the noisy `black` variable and a cross-axis `female` substitute, but here the substituting variable is `female` predicting gender inequality — the cleanest, best-measured, perfectly on-axis standpoint in the design — and it still interacts negatively with field, indicating genuine structural saturation rather than noise. Race and gender producing identical interaction signatures, with the same three terms, same order, and same signs, elevates the framework from an outcome-specific account to a general property of the science system: disciplinary context combines with contextual inputs as complements and with portable author-identity dispositions as substitutes, because field membership functions as institutional permission whose presence both enables the temporal wave and renders redundant the author's own orientation. The governing assumption is therefore that interaction sign is determined not by which inequality axis is at stake, nor by how well a feature is measured, but by the structural relationship between the feature and disciplinary legitimacy — complementary contextual forces yield positive interactions, substitutable identity dispositions yield negative ones — and that this holds invariantly across racial and gender discourse alike.

However, the negative `female × social_science` interaction means that female authorship and social-science location do not simply reinforce each other. Instead, female authorship may have its largest marginal effect outside social science, where it more strongly signals a gender-sensitive, critical, or inequality-oriented research agenda. Inside social science, gender inequality is already sufficiently legitimate and common as a research topic, so additional female authorship contributes less incremental predictive power. Thus, the theory is one of complementarity between field and discourse, but partial substitution between field and gendered author standpoint.
